caption:
Did Daniel Dunglas Home really float out of a window?

In 1868, in front of three witnesses — Lord Adare, Captain Wynne and Lord Lindsay — Home was said to have levitated out of a third-storey window and back in through the next one. It made him one of the most famous men of his era.

The witnesses could not agree on anything. Adare said the street was 70 feet down; Lindsay said 85; Home said 80. Adare said it was dark; Lindsay said bright moonlight. Adare said the third floor, then the first. Trevor H. Hall placed it at Ashley Place, Westminster, at 35 feet, with a four-foot gap between two iron balconies. Gordon Stein agreed the gap was crossable on foot. Joseph McCabe noted nobody claims to have watched Home travel between the windows — and that a nineteen-inch sill ran outside. Days earlier, Home had opened that same window and stood on the ledge in front of two witnesses.

Home was privately caught cheating more than once. A sitter at Ealing in 1855 said the "spirit hand" was a false limb on Home's arm. In Biarritz in 1857, a physician's letter described Home slipping off a thin shoe and working the room with his bare foot.

William Crookes, FRS, tested him anyway, and published that the phenomena were genuine. His accordion cage experiment ran under a dining table in unstated light. Podmore noted nobody ever saw the keys move. Home's accordion only ever played two tunes: Home Sweet Home and The Last Rose of Summer. Both fit in one octave.

Still unresolved: Home was never publicly exposed, and no explanation of the window has ever been proved.

Portraits by Nadar and the Atelier Nadar; a c.1868 portrait by the London Stereoscopic & Photographic Company; engravings from Crookes, Paris 1878.
